contract: template<unsigned BITS> struct RefCount { void acquire(); bool release(); };  starts at 1; acquire() is only called by a thread that already holds a reference; release() returns true exactly when the caller dropped the last reference and must destroy the object.
instantiate: template struct RefCount<3>; template struct RefCount<32>;
harness_note: the workers' writes to the object are plain ints, so the destroyer missing a happens-before edge is a data race
statement: Main and T worker threads share an object; each worker writes its part while holding a reference, may clone and drop extra references, then releases. Exactly one release reports 'last'; that release sees every write made before any release; nobody touches the object after it is freed; no data race; every operation returns. In addition, the count honours BITS: it must hold at least 2^BITS - 2 references normally, and when more are taken it must saturate before it could wrap: after that it never reaches zero and no release reports 'last' (the object is leaked, never freed while references are alive).
scenario_rule: a 2-bit scenario that uses exactly the promised capacity (2^BITS - 2 references) and must free normally, a shrunk 3-bit scenario below saturation, and overflow scenarios whose total reference count is 1 modulo 2^BITS (2-bit: 1 + 1 + 3 = 5), so that a wrapping counter lands exactly where a release reads 1 and frees the object while references are alive

survivor_annotations.why: moves the saturation point one value later (2^BITS instead of 2^BITS - 1). The count is stored in a full unsigned, so it still saturates before it can ever wrap: no early free is possible. The spec deliberately constrains safety (never free early, leak after overflow) and the promised minimum capacity, not the exact saturation value

liveness_note: non-blocking contract; GenMC's spin-loop liveness heuristic misreports CAS retry loops, so termination is checked instead
